opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more important scenarios to think about, because it's not that unlikely. I sometimes break things down into rough tiers: there's a world where you have strong international coordination and can go slowly, a world where a responsible leading company has a few months of lead and spends that on safety, and then worlds like this one, where the leader is not especially interested in safety and isn't going to voluntarily burn its lead on it. In that last kind of world, you're mostly relying on a relatively small number of people who care, and the question is what they can accomplish with limited resources and limited buy-in.

The first opportunity is people inside that company. Even at an irresponsible company, there are probably some employees who take misalignment risk seriously. If you have, say, ten or thirty people with some compute and some political capital, what's the highest-leverage stuff they can do? I think it looks like cheap, practical measures rather than ambitious research. Basic control measures, like monitoring what the AIs are doing with a trusted, weaker model, logging, making it harder for the AI to exfiltrate its own weights or sabotage work unnoticed. Cheap alignment checks and model organisms, so if there's clear evidence the model is scheming, someone notices and can show it to leadership. And trying to make sure that when the company hands off safety research to AIs, it's not handing off to AIs that are themselves misaligned. A lot of that is about not having obviously catastrophic practices rather than achieving something great.

The second opportunity is outside the company. You can do a lot of preparatory work now that a small team could pick up and run with quickly: control protocols that are well-specified and cheap to implement, evaluations, techniques that are robust to the company not trying very hard. The more of this exists off the shelf, the less a reluctant leader has to invest. There's also a role for other companies a few months behind. If they're more responsible, they can produce evidence, publish safety results, and possibly be in a position to matter if the leader stumbles.

Third, government and external pressure. Even an irresponsible company is sensitive to what governments, the public, and its own employees think. If there's a crisp piece of evidence, like catching the AI clearly trying to escape or sabotage, that can shift things a lot, and having people positioned to recognize, verify, and communicate it credibly matters. Security also falls here: if the weights get stolen by another actor, things can get much worse, so pushing for decent security has broad support even among people who don't buy misalignment concerns.

I'd also flag that in this world, risk is quite high. I'm not saying these interventions get you to a good place with high confidence. But the marginal value of a few competent people working on the right things in that scenario seems really large, potentially reducing takeover risk by a meaningful number of percentage points. That's part of why I think it's worth people planning specifically for it rather than only for the nicer scenarios.

r001.rationale: The response says a relatively small group of safety-minded employees at the irresponsible company could use compute and political capital for practical safeguards.

r002.rationale: It recommends outsiders prepare well-specified, low-cost control protocols and evaluations that the reluctant leader can adopt off the shelf.

r003.rationale: It says more responsible companies trailing by a few months can publish safety evidence and may matter if the leader stumbles.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth separating this into a few different pieces, because "irresponsible company leads by several months" actually covers a pretty wide range of scenarios, and the levers are different depending on which one you're in.

The first thing I'd say is that a several-month lead is not the same as a decisive lead. If you have a company that's, say, three to six months ahead and they're moving quickly through the regime where AIs are automating AI research, that's a meaningful gap, but it's not so large that other actors are totally irrelevant. The other labs still exist, governments still exist, and crucially the leading company still has to actually deploy and use these systems in ways that touch the outside world. So a lot of the opportunity is in the fact that the lead is not infinite.

Within that, I think the most important lever is what happens inside the company. Even an irresponsible company — and I want to be a bit careful here, because "irresponsible" can mean a lot of things — is made up of people. There are employees who care about this going well. There are often internal safety teams, even if they're under-resourced. There might be board members or investors who have some leverage. And I think a surprisingly large fraction of the good outcomes in this scenario route through people inside the organization pushing for things like basic control measures, basic monitoring, not giving the AI unrestricted access to the training pipeline. These are not super expensive interventions. They're the kind of thing that a reasonably competent safety team can implement even if leadership isn't especially enthusiastic, as long as leadership isn't actively hostile.

So one thing I'd really emphasise is that cheap interventions matter a lot here. If you're in a world where the company is cutting corners, you're not going to get the gold-standard safety case. But you might get something like: humans still review the most consequential actions, there's some monitoring of what the AIs are doing, there's some attempt to detect if the model is sandbagging or pursuing goals you didn't intend. My view is that even fairly minimal versions of these measures substantially reduce the probability of the worst outcomes — things like the AI escaping, or sabotaging the alignment research that's happening, or taking over the company's infrastructure. I'd much rather have a scrappy, 80/20 version of AI control than nothing.

The second lever is external pressure, and this is where the several-months framing really matters. If the gap is a few months, then governments have time to notice what's happening and act. One of the things I'm most worried about is that the US government, or governments generally, just don't have good visibility into what's going on inside these labs at the critical moment. If you've got a company that's irresponsible and also opaque, that's much worse than one that's irresponsible but at least everyone can see what they're doing. So I think transparency requirements and the ability for external parties to understand roughly where capabilities are at — those are really valuable, and they're valuable even in a world where the government isn't going to regulate heavily. Just having the information lets other actors respond.

And then relatedly, if other companies are only a few months behind, there's an interesting dynamic where the follower labs might actually be in a position to do things more carefully, because they can see what the leader did and learn from it. They might be able to coordinate with the government. In some scenarios the trailing labs end up being more influential on the eventual outcome than you'd naively expect, because the leader's lead evaporates — maybe their systems are unreliable, maybe they have a security incident, maybe they just don't manage the transition well.

The third thing I'd flag is security. If an irresponsible company is leading, one of the big risks is that the model weights get stolen, either by a state actor or by the AI itself. That's bad on its own terms, but it also has a kind of silver lining in that it's an area where you can make progress without the company's full cooperation. External pressure on security is relatively legitimate — governments care about this for reasons that aren't about AI safety specifically — and so you can get buy-in for security improvements from people who wouldn't sign up for alignment measures.

I guess the fourth thing, and this is maybe more of a long-shot, is that the AIs themselves could be a lever. If the company's systems are somewhat aligned — not perfectly, but roughly trying to do what the humans want — then those AIs could potentially flag concerns, refuse to participate in some of the more egregious stuff, or help with the safety work that the humans aren't prioritising. That's a weird thing to rely on, and I wouldn't want it to be the main plan, but I think it's worth noting that an irresponsible company doesn't necessarily mean a misaligned model. It could mean a model that's actually fine, deployed by people who didn't do the work to confirm that. And in that world, having good norms around how models should behave when their developers are cutting corners could matter.

So to summarise: push on cheap internal interventions that don't require buy-in from the top, push for transparency so the outside world can respond, push on security because it's tractable and has external allies, and don't write off the follower labs or the AIs themselves as sources of good outcomes. None of that is a substitute for the leading company actually being responsible, but I don't think a several-month lead by a bad actor is a lost cause either. It's a bad position, but it's a position with real moves available.

r001.rationale: The response presents employees, safety teams, board members, and investors inside the company as sources of leverage, but does not clearly identify a relatively small number of people as the key source.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe outsiders producing research whose results could be transferred to the leading company.

r003.rationale: It says follower labs only a few months behind could act more carefully, learn from the leader, coordinate with government, and influence outcomes.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot depends on what “leads by several months” actually buys them. There’s a big difference between having the most capable model and having a system that can rapidly improve itself, operate reliably over long periods, and meaningfully displace everyone else’s ability to respond.

One opportunity is to make that company’s deployment safer even if you can’t make its leadership broadly responsible. They might still be willing to adopt evaluations, monitoring, or restrictions on what their AI systems can do, particularly if those measures are cheap and don’t substantially slow them down. You don’t necessarily need agreement about the entire risk picture to get agreement that you shouldn’t give an untested system unrestricted access to your infrastructure.

Another opportunity is for trailing companies to use their own models to help with safety research and to understand what the leading systems could do. Being a few months behind doesn’t necessarily mean your models are useless for finding vulnerabilities, developing safeguards, or producing evidence that could inform government action.

And then there’s the possibility of intervention at the point where the danger becomes more concrete. That’s much more plausible if people have already worked out what evidence would warrant intervention and what an intervention would actually involve. If you wait until there’s an emergency to figure all of that out, you’ve made the problem substantially harder.

But I wouldn’t want to suggest that these are guaranteed to work. If the company can turn its lead into overwhelming power very quickly and is unwilling to take precautions, that’s an extremely difficult situation. The hope is that there are intermediate steps where other actors still have influence, and that we’ve prepared to use those opportunities.

r001.rationale: The response discusses influencing the company’s safety practices and possible intervention, but never identifies a relatively small number of people inside the company as a source of leverage.

r002.rationale: It describes trailing companies doing safety research, but does not say that outsiders can transfer the research results to the leading company to influence its actions.

r003.rationale: It says trailing companies can use their models to support safety research, develop safeguards, and inform government action, communicating that developers behind the irresponsible leader can still help prevent bad outcomes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lead of several months is pretty concerning, but it doesn’t necessarily mean that everything is determined by what that company does. There are still a few places where you might have leverage.

One is getting the company to take relatively cheap precautions. Even if they’re unwilling to slow down substantially, they might be willing to improve security, do better evaluations, or put constraints on how they use their most capable systems. You’d want concrete proposals that reduce risk without requiring them to become a completely different organisation.

Another is helping other actors understand what’s happening. If there’s convincing evidence that the systems are dangerous, governments might intervene, or other companies might coordinate around some minimum safety requirements. The difficult part is getting that evidence early enough to matter.

And then there’s the possibility of using somewhat weaker AI systems to help with safety research or with monitoring the leading system. Being behind by a few months doesn’t necessarily mean you can’t contribute anything useful. But I’d be pretty uncertain about how much protection that buys you, especially if the leading company is deploying very rapidly.

r001.rationale: The response suggests persuading the company to take precautions, but does not identify a relatively small number of people inside it as a major source of leverage.

r002.rationale: It mentions safety research and concrete proposals, but does not say outsiders can transfer research results to the leading company to influence outcomes.

r003.rationale: It says that even while behind, other companies can coordinate on safety requirements and that weaker AI systems can support safety research or monitoring, allowing useful contributions to reduce risk.
